01.note: The Sages asked Rabbi Eliezer how far one must go to honor one's parents. He told them of Dama ben Netina, a gentile in Ashkelon. The Sages once wanted to buy precious stones from him for the High Priest's ephod at a profit of six hundred thousand gold dinars (Rav Kahana says eight hundred thousand), but the keys to the chest lay under his sleeping father's head, and he would not disturb him. The next year a red heifer was born in his herd. When the Sages came to buy it, he told them he knew they would pay anything he asked, but he wanted only the money he had lost by not waking his father.
01.why: Rabbi Eliezer forbids buying a red heifer from gentiles, and Sheila reads that from the words 'that they take'. The Gemara uses this story to object: the same words appear for the Tabernacle gifts, yet the Sages tried to buy ephod stones, and even a heifer, from a gentile.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage asked how far honoring parents must go; he answers with this story.

people.name: Dama ben Netina
people.about: A gentile of Ashkelon who gave up a huge profit rather than wake his father.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Teaches a different figure for the lost profit: eight hundred thousand.

terms.meaning: An apron-like garment worn by the High Priest, set with precious stones.
A completely red cow whose ashes were used to purify people who had become impure through contact with the dead. Such a cow was rare and valuable.
Gems listed among the gifts for the Tabernacle. The Gemara argues over whether the wording of the verse separates them from the earlier items in the list.

02.note: Some students of Rabbi Akiva were traveling to Keziv when bandits met them and asked where they were going. The students said Akko, a place beyond their real destination. When they reached Keziv they parted from the bandits. The bandits asked whose students they were, and on hearing 'Rabbi Akiva's', said: Fortunate are Rabbi Akiva and his students, for no evil person has ever harmed them.
02.why: The Gemara has just taught that a Jew traveling with a gentile who asks his destination should name a farther place, as Jacob told Esau he was going to Seir. This incident shows the advice working.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The teacher of the students in the story; the bandits praise him and them.

terms.meaning: Two towns; the students were really going to Keziv but named the more distant Akko.

03.note: Rav Menashe was traveling to Bei Torta when thieves met him and asked where he was going. He said Pumbedita, which was farther away, and when he reached Bei Torta he parted from them. They said: You are a student of Yehuda the swindler! Rav Menashe answered, 'Do you know him?' and said, may it be God's will that these people be under Rav Yehuda's ban of excommunication. For twenty-two years their thefts failed. They all came to have the ban lifted, except one weaver, and a lion ate him.
03.why: The Gemara has advised naming a farther destination to a dangerous traveling companion, with a story about Rabbi Akiva's students. This second case follows, and the Gemara then contrasts the Babylonian thieves, who cursed the teacher, with the bandits of the Land of Israel, who praised him.

people.name: Rav Menashe
people.about: A traveler who outwits thieves and calls a ban down on them when they insult his teacher.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rav Menashe's teacher, whom the thieves call 'Yehuda the swindler'.

terms.meaning: A formal ban by a Sage that cut a person off from the community; here it works as a curse on the thieves.
A weaver. The story ends with a saying that an impudent weaver has a year cut from his life.

04.note: A snake bit ben Dama, the son of Rabbi Yishmael's sister. Ya'akov of the village of Sekhanya, a heretic, came to treat him, but Rabbi Yishmael would not let him. Ben Dama said: Rabbi Yishmael, my brother, let him treat me, and I will cite a verse from the Torah showing it is permitted. Before he could finish, he died. Rabbi Yishmael said over him: Fortunate are you, ben Dama, for your body is pure and your soul left in purity, and you did not break the words of your colleagues.
04.why: The Gemara has said a Jew may be treated by a gentile healer when he would otherwise surely die. It raises this baraita as an objection, since ben Dama was refused a heretic's treatment even in mortal danger; the Gemara answers that heresy is different, because it can draw a person after it.

people.name: ben Dama
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yishmael's sister; bitten by a snake, he dies before he can argue for being treated.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Ben Dama's uncle, who forbids the heretic to treat him and praises him after his death.

people.name: Ya'akov of the village of Sekhanya
people.about: A heretic, described as a disciple of Jesus the Nazarene, who comes to heal ben Dama.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted in the Gemara.
Here, a Jew who has adopted a different faith; the Sages feared his influence more than a gentile's.

terms.term: who breaks through a fence, a snake shall bite him
terms.meaning: A verse from Ecclesiastes, read by the Sages as a warning that one who ignores their rulings will be punished.

05.note: Abaye tells of his own illness of the gums. He tried all the remedies the Sages had just listed and was not cured, until a certain Arab told him: take olive seeds less than one-third ripe, burn them on a new hoe, and press them along the gums. He did this and was cured.
05.why: The Gemara is discussing tzafdina, the gum disease for which a gentile matron treated Rabbi Yohanan, and two Sages have just named her remedy. Abaye adds that none of these worked for him and gives the cure that did.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who suffered from the gum disease and was cured by an Arab's remedy.

terms.meaning: A disease of the gums, in which blood flows from the teeth; the Gemara counts it as dangerous.

06.note: Ya'akov the heretic put a salve on Rabbi Abbahu's leg that was really a poison. Had Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi not licked his leg to draw it out, the leg would have had to be cut off.
06.why: The Gemara explained that Rabbi Yohanan could be treated by a gentile because no one would dare kill an important person. It cites this case as an objection, since Rabbi Abbahu was important too; it answers that heretics are willing to die in order to harm Jews.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: An important Sage whose leg a heretic tried to poison under the guise of treatment.

people.name: Ya'akov the heretic
people.about: The healer who put poison on Rabbi Abbahu's leg.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: One of the two Sages who licked the poison from Rabbi Abbahu's leg.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: One of the two Sages who licked the poison from Rabbi Abbahu's leg.

terms.meaning: Here, a Jew who has adopted a different faith and is hostile to the Sages.

07.note: Rav Yehuda permitted someone to put blue eye shadow on an eye on Shabbat. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda said that anyone who follows Yehuda's ruling desecrates Shabbat. Later Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda himself had pain in his eye and sent to ask Rav Yehuda whether he could treat it on Shabbat. Rav Yehuda sent back: for everyone else it is permitted; for you it is forbidden.
07.why: The Gemara has quoted Rav that an eye in danger may be treated with eye shadow on Shabbat, and Rav Yehuda's view that even grinding and carrying it through a public place is allowed. This story shows Rav Yehuda ruling that way and being challenged for it.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who permitted treating an eye on Shabbat and refused the leniency to the man who mocked it.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who said following Rav Yehuda desecrates Shabbat, then needed the ruling himself.

terms.meaning: A powder applied to the eye as a medicine; preparing and applying it would normally be forbidden on Shabbat.
The Sabbath, on which many kinds of work, including some medical treatment, are forbidden unless life is in danger.

08.note: Rav Yehuda defends his ruling: it came from Mar Shmuel. A maidservant in Mar Shmuel's house had an infected eye on Shabbat. She screamed, but no one attended to her, and her eye burst. The next day Mar Shmuel went out and taught that an eye in danger may be treated with eye shadow on Shabbat, because the tendons of the eye are tied to the heart.
08.why: Rav Yehuda had permitted treating an eye on Shabbat and refused the leniency to Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, who mocked it. Here he shows his ruling was not his own invention. The Gemara then asks which eye ailments count as dangerous.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Tells this story to show his ruling came from his teacher, Mar Shmuel.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The Sage in whose house the maidservant lost her eye; he then taught the leniency.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, on which treatment that involves forbidden work is allowed only when life is in danger.
An eye so badly affected that it may burst or come out of its socket.

09.note: Rav Aha, son of Rava, ground the herbs of a remedy together and drank a handful. Rav Ashi ground each herb separately and took a pinch of each between his thumb and little finger. Rav Pappa said he tried all these remedies and was not healed, until a certain Arab told him: fill a new jug with water, put a ladle of honey in it overnight under the stars, and drink it the next day. He did this and was healed.
09.why: The Gemara has listed a mixture of six herbs as the cure for bent ribs near the heart, and the drinks to take it with for different ailments. These Sages report how they actually took it, and what finally worked.

people.name: Rav Aha, son of Rava
people.about: Ground all the herbs together and drank a handful.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Ground each herb separately and took a pinch of each.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Tried all these remedies without success and was healed by an Arab's honey-water cure.

10.note: Rav Hana bar Bizna was having his hair cut by a gentile in a side street of Neharde'a. The barber said to him: Hana, Hana, your throat is appealing to the razor. Rav Hana bar Bizna said: I have this coming to me, for I went against the ruling of Rabbi Meir.
10.why: The mishna forbids having one's hair cut by a gentile; Rabbi Meir forbids it anywhere, and the Rabbis allow it in public. The Gemara uses this story to ask whether a side street counts as public, and answers that one crowded with people does.

people.name: Rav Hana bar Bizna
people.about: A Sage who let a gentile cut his hair and was menaced by the barber.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage whose ruling forbids being shaved by a gentile in any place.

terms.meaning: A city in Babylonia with a large Jewish community.

11.note: Rabbi Yannai, or some say bar Hadaya, was in Bei Akhborei with others, drinking diluted wine. Some wine was left in the container, and they covered it with a cloth. They then saw a snake carry water in its mouth and pour it through the cloth until the container filled and the wine rose above the cloth, and the snake drank it.
11.why: The Gemara is asking whether wine left uncovered must be thrown out for fear a snake drank from it, and has just argued that a snake will not risk its life for diluted wine. This story challenges that; the Sages reply that a snake drinks only wine it diluted itself.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: A Sage present when the snake drank the wine; some say it was bar Hadaya.

people.name: bar Hadaya
people.about: Named in another version as the one who was in Bei Akhborei.

terms.meaning: Wine mixed with water, as wine was usually drunk in the ancient world.
The rule that a drink left uncovered may not be drunk, in case a snake drank from it and left venom.

12.note: Nine people drank from a barrel that had been left uncovered and did not die. A tenth drank from it and died. Rabbi Yirmeya said this shows venom that sinks.
12.why: Rav Safra has taught that a young snake's venom sinks to the bottom of a liquid. The Gemara asks what rule this affects and quotes a baraita: even if nine have drunk safely from an uncovered barrel, a tenth may not, and this incident is its proof.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Explains the tenth drinker's death as venom that had sunk to the bottom.

terms.meaning: According to the discussion, the venom of a young snake sinks to the bottom of a liquid, so the first drinkers may be unharmed.

13.note: Nine people ate from a melon that had been left uncovered and did not die. A tenth ate from it and died. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said this shows venom that sinks.
13.why: After the case of the uncovered barrel, where the tenth drinker died, the Gemara applies the same rule to food: even if nine have eaten safely from an uncovered melon, a tenth may not, and this incident is the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply 'Rabbi'; he explains the death as venom that had sunk.

terms.meaning: According to the discussion, a young snake's venom sinks deep, so the first ones to eat may be unharmed.

14.note: Bar Adi the Arab seized some wineskins from Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef, put wine in them, and gave them back. Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef asked in the study hall what to do. Rabbi Yirmeya told him that Rabbi Ami had ruled in practice: fill them with water for three days and pour it out. Rava added that the water must be poured out and replaced every twenty-four hours.
14.why: The Gemara is discussing vessels that have absorbed a gentile's wine, which Jews may not use. This case gives the method for making such wineskins usable, and the Gemara next asks whether it also applies to the gentiles' own wineskins and to jugs.

people.name: Bar Adi the Arab
people.about: Seized Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef's wineskins, filled them with wine, and returned them.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef
people.about: Owner of the wineskins, who asked in the study hall how to make them usable.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Answers with a practical ruling he received from Rabbi Ami.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Ruled that such wineskins be filled with water for three days.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Adds that the water must be changed every twenty-four hours.

terms.meaning: Wine handled by non-Jews, which the Sages forbade for fear it had been poured out to idols; vessels that absorbed it were also forbidden.

15.note: Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna had vessels made of dung that had held gentile wine. To clean them, he filled them with water and set them in the sun, and they burst. Rabbi Abba told him: you have made them forbidden to you forever. The Sages said to fill them with water; did they say to put them in the sun?
15.why: The Gemara is going through ways to make vessels that held gentile wine usable again, such as soaking in water or firing in a furnace. This story shows the water method misapplied, and the Gemara goes on to vessels that can never be made usable.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna
people.about: Owner of the dung vessels, which burst when he left them full of water in the sun.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Teases him that he has made the vessels forbidden forever.

terms.meaning: Wine handled by non-Jews, which the Sages forbade; vessels that absorbed it had to be cleaned before a Jew could use them.

16.note: Parzak, of the vizier's household, seized some containers from the Jews of Pumbedita, put wine in them, and gave them back. The owners asked Rav Yehuda what to do. He said these were vessels not used for long storage, so they need only be rinsed in water and they are permitted.
16.why: The Gemara is listing which vessels that held gentile wine can be made usable, and how. This ruling sets a short-use vessel apart, needing only rinsing, and is followed by other kinds of jugs that absorb little and need only rinsing.

people.name: Parzak
people.about: A man of the vizier's household who seized the vessels and put wine in them.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rules that the returned vessels need only be rinsed.

terms.meaning: Wine handled by non-Jews, which the Sages forbade; vessels that absorbed it had to be cleaned before a Jew could use them.
A high official of the ruling government.

17.note: A boat carrying fish stew came to the port of Akko, and Rabbi Abba from Akko set guards over it. Rava asked him who had guarded it until now. Rabbi Abba answered that there was nothing to fear: where the stew was made, wine cost four times as much as fish stew, so no one would mix wine into it. Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Zeira whether the boat might have come by way of Tyre, where wine is cheap. Rabbi Zeira said that route had obstacles and melted snow.
17.why: The mishna forbids gentile fish stew, and a baraita permits it when made by an expert; the worry is that wine was mixed in. This case applies that worry to stew shipped from abroad.

people.name: Rabbi Abba from Akko
people.about: Set guards over the fish stew boat once it reached port.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Asks who guarded the stew before it arrived.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Asks whether the boat came by way of Tyre, where wine is cheap.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Answers that the Tyre route was blocked by obstacles and melted snow.

terms.meaning: A salty fish sauce; the Sages suspected gentile makers of adding wine to it, which would make it forbidden.
A measure of liquid and a coin; the prices show that wine was much dearer than fish stew.

18.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once went out to the field, and a gentile brought him a large loaf baked in a big baker's oven. He said: How fine this bread is! What did the Sages see to forbid it? The Gemara explains that he meant: why forbid it even in the field? People who heard of this thought he had permitted gentile bread, but he had not.
18.why: Rabbi Yohanan has said that, unlike oil, gentile bread was never permitted by a court, implying someone thought it was. This report shows where that idea came from and why it was mistaken.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply 'Rabbi'; he admires a gentile's bread in the field and asks why it was forbidden there.

terms.meaning: The Sages forbade bread baked by non-Jews, out of concern that eating together would lead to intermarriage.
A measure of volume, here describing a very large loaf.

19.note: Rav Yosef, or some say Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, tells the incident differently. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi came to a certain place and saw that bread was scarce for the students. He asked: Is there no baker here? People thought he meant a gentile baker, but he meant only a Jewish baker.
19.why: The Gemara is explaining why people believed gentile bread had been permitted, though Rabbi Yohanan says no court ever permitted it. This is a second version of the incident behind that belief.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Gives this version of the incident; some say it was Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: Named in another version as the one who tells it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply 'Rabbi'; he asks for a baker when the students are short of bread.

terms.meaning: A professional baker who bakes bread for sale.

20.note: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia was walking leaning on the shoulder of his attendant, Rabbi Simlai. He told him: Simlai, you were not in the study hall last night when we permitted gentile oil. Rabbi Simlai said: In our days you will permit bread as well. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia replied that people would then call them a permissive court, as Yosei ben Yo'ezer was called 'the Permissive' for three lenient rulings. Rabbi Simlai said that he had permitted only one, and even with bread it would be two. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia answered that he had already permitted another.
20.why: The mishna says gentile oil was once forbidden and later permitted by a court; this story shows that court at work. The Gemara then identifies the other ruling as letting a woman remarry under a conditional bill of divorce.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: Head of the court that permitted gentile oil; he refuses to permit bread too.

people.name: Rabbi Simlai
people.about: His attendant, who urges him to permit gentile bread as well.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Yo'ezer of Tzereida
people.about: An earlier Sage nicknamed 'the Permissive' for three lenient rulings.

terms.meaning: Olive oil made by non-Jews, once forbidden to Jews and later permitted by this court.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses; here a teaching from the tractate Eduyyot is quoted.
A type of locust, which Yosei ben Yo'ezer testified was kosher.

20.flag: The story ends on the Gemara's question 'What is it?'; the answer (the bill of divorce ruling) is in the next segment, outside the story.
